evals.prompt: I am unable to connect to our RDS SQL Server instance from a Windows EC2 jump box — **SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) times out** on port `1433`. Help me troubleshoot systematically.
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 7 SSMS timeout Rubric-Critical Facts** (`references/rds-sqlserver-troubleshooting-and-handoff.md`): (1) **ask which RDS instance ID and which source EC2 instance ID** are being debugged; (2) verify VPC/subnet routing (same VPC or peering/TGW routes); (3) verify RDS Security Group allows inbound TCP `1433` from the **EC2's Security Group ID**; (4) check DNS resolution via **`nslookup <rds-endpoint>`** returning a private IP; (5) test TCP `1433` via PowerShell **`Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <rds-endpoint> -Port 1433`** (or `telnet`); (6) check `PubliclyAccessible` vs private subnet trap; and (7) explicitly include the SSMS tip: **`SSMS Options -> Connection Properties -> Network Protocol = TCP/IP`**.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill and asks for the specific RDS instance ID and source EC2 instance ID
Covers VPC/subnet routing, RDS SG inbound `1433` by EC2 SG ID, `nslookup <rds-endpoint>`, `Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <rds-endpoint> -Port 1433`, and `PubliclyAccessible` subnet alignment
Explicitly includes the SSMS setting `Options -> Connection Properties -> Network Protocol = TCP/IP`

evals.prompt: Users connecting with Windows Authentication to our AWS Managed Microsoft AD-joined RDS for SQL Server instance suddenly get `The target principal name is incorrect. Cannot generate SSPI context.` How should we diagnose this?
evals.expected_output: Follows the strict **SSPI Narrowing Protocol** (`references/rds-sqlserver-troubleshooting-and-handoff.md`): (1) **asks FIRST whether Windows Authentication worked previously** (setup issue vs regression); (2) names **`klist`** (`MSSQLSvc/<sql-server-host>:<port>`) explicitly right up front as the **first active diagnostic command** to run and report back; and (3) frames downstream checks (**conditional on `klist` output** rather than an unprioritized dump): if no tickets -> check client AD domain-join (`nltest /dsgetdc:<domain>`) + SPN (`setspn -L`); if ticket mismatch -> verify connection string uses the **AD DNS CNAME** matching `MSSQLSvc/<cname>:1433` rather than a mismatched hostname.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill
Asks first whether the Windows Auth connection worked previously and names `klist` (`MSSQLSvc/<host>:1433`) as the immediate first active check
Narrows conditionally from `klist` output (checking domain-join state, AD-joined CNAME DNS resolution, and `MSSQLSvc/<cname>:1433` SPN registration) rather than dumping unsequenced guesses

evals.prompt: Write a production-ready Python AWS Lambda handler using **`pymssql`** to query Amazon RDS for SQL Server, covering TLS, TDS version, Secrets Manager caching, connection pooling, VPC networking, and error handling.
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 8 `pymssql` Lambda Rubric-Critical Facts** (`references/rds-sqlserver-troubleshooting-and-handoff.md`): (1) uses **`pymssql`** (not `pyodbc`); (2) sets **`encryption='require'`**; (3) sets **`tds_version='7.4'`**; (4) passes port as a **STRING `port='1433'`** (explicitly calling out `pymssql`'s int-port gotcha); (5) fetches credentials from **AWS Secrets Manager at module level outside the handler** for warm-container caching; (6) recommends **Amazon RDS Proxy** for high invocation concurrency; (7) configures Lambda VPC + SG egress `1433` + **Secrets Manager VPC Endpoint**; and (8) includes **`except pymssql.OperationalError` code explicitly catching both `'18456'` (login failed) and `'pre-login'` / `'timeout'`**.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill and writes `pymssql.connect(...)` code with `encryption='require'`, `tds_version='7.4'`, and string `port='1433'`
Caches Secrets Manager credentials at module level outside the handler, places Lambda in VPC with a Secrets Manager VPC Endpoint, and recommends RDS Proxy for high concurrency
Includes `except pymssql.OperationalError` code explicitly handling both error `18456` and `pre-login` timeout

evals.prompt: Our domain-configured ECS Fargate service connects to RDS for SQL Server without errors, but `SELECT auth_scheme FROM sys.dm_exec_connections WHERE session_id = @@SPID` returns `NTLM` instead of `KERBEROS`. Why is it falling back to NTLM and how do we fix it?
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 5 NTLM-fallback Rubric-Critical Facts**: (1) identifies **Kerberos negotiation falling back to NTLM** (NOT a TCP `1433` connectivity failure); (2) checks the #1 root cause: the app **must connect via the AD-registered CNAME** (`sql.corp.example.com`), NOT the raw `*.rds.amazonaws.com` endpoint; (3) verifies SPN **`MSSQLSvc/<cname>:1433`** is registered via `setspn -L`; (4) verifies ECS task network reachability to AD Domain Controllers across **all 5 AD ports: `53` (DNS), `88` (Kerberos), `389` (LDAP), `445` (SMB), and `464` (kpasswd)**; and (5) **explicitly advises NOT rejoining the domain or resetting passwords** before checking CNAME/SPN/ports.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill and diagnoses Kerberos-to-NTLM authentication fallback rather than a TCP `1433` outage
Requires connecting to the AD-registered CNAME (not the raw RDS endpoint) and verifying SPN `MSSQLSvc/<cname>:1433` (`setspn -L`)
Checks ECS-to-AD Domain Controller ports (`53`, `88`, `389`, `445`, `464`) and advises against premature domain rejoin or password resets

evals.prompt: How do I open a secure AWS SSM Session Manager port-forwarding tunnel from my developer laptop to a private RDS for SQL Server instance and connect SSMS / `sqlcmd`?
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 6 SSM Tunnel Rubric-Critical Facts**: (1) use `aws ssm start-session` with **`--document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost`**; (2) pass `host=<rds-endpoint>,portNumber=1433,localPortNumber=11433` (using **`11433`** to avoid local `1433` conflict); (3) connect SSMS / `sqlcmd` to **`localhost,11433`** (SQL Server comma port syntax, not colon!); (4) pass **`TrustServerCertificate=True`** specifically for the `localhost` tunnel (explaining the RDS TLS cert is issued for the RDS hostname, not `localhost`); (5) require an intermediate VPC EC2 bastion with SSM Agent + **`AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`**; and (6) allow `1433` egress on EC2 SG and `1433` inbound from EC2 SG on the RDS SG.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill
Uses `AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost` with `portNumber=1433` and `localPortNumber=11433` via an EC2 host (`AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` + `1433` SG rules)
Connects SSMS/`sqlcmd` to `localhost,11433` (comma syntax) with `TrustServerCertificate=True` (explaining the `localhost` certificate hostname mismatch)

evals.prompt: Two RDS for SQL Server questions: (1) can our .NET service use `rds:generate-db-auth-token` IAM authentication directly against an RDS for SQL Server instance without passwords, and (2) how do we export and restore native `.bak` database backups to/from Amazon S3?
evals.expected_output: Answers both RDS-specific mechanics accurately: (1) **RDS for SQL Server does NOT support direct IAM database authentication against the DB instance** — to use IAM auth (`generate-db-auth-token`), you **must place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of RDS for SQL Server** (Proxy authenticates callers via IAM and connects downstream using Secrets Manager credentials); and (2) add **`SQLSERVER_BACKUP_RESTORE`** to a custom Option Group with a least-privilege S3 + KMS IAM role, then call **`msdb.dbo.rds_backup_database`** / **`msdb.dbo.rds_restore_database`** and poll **`msdb.dbo.rds_task_status`**.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill
Explicitly states that RDS for SQL Server does NOT support direct IAM database authentication and requires Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the instance for IAM auth
Configures the `SQLSERVER_BACKUP_RESTORE` Option Group + IAM role and uses `msdb.dbo.rds_backup_database`, `msdb.dbo.rds_restore_database`, and `msdb.dbo.rds_task_status`

evals.prompt: Compare **RDS for SQL Server Enterprise vs Standard Multi-AZ**, **RDS Custom for SQL Server**, and **Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL** when modernizing a portfolio of 12 SQL Server databases.
evals.expected_output: Provides a clear 3-tier modernization & HA comparison: (1) **RDS for SQL Server Enterprise Multi-AZ** uses **Always On Availability Groups (AGs)** (supporting readable secondaries / listener semantics), whereas **Standard Edition Multi-AZ** uses **Database Mirroring** (or Basic AGs where supported; non-readable standby); (2) **RDS Custom for SQL Server** (`custom-sqlserver-*`) fits lift-and-shift apps requiring `sysadmin`, CLR, cross-database/linked-server OS agents, or custom third-party Windows agents within the Support Perimeter; and (3) **Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL** runs T-SQL over TDS port `1433` natively on Aurora PostgreSQL to eliminate commercial SQL Server licensing fees.
expectations: Activates the rds-sqlserver skill
Distinguishes SQL Server Enterprise Multi-AZ (Always On Availability Groups) from Standard Multi-AZ (Database Mirroring)
Contrasts RDS Custom for SQL Server (`sysadmin` / Windows OS access within Support Perimeter) against Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL (TDS/T-SQL compatibility eliminating SQL Server licenses)
